screens.narratorSegment: As your AWS footprint grows, individual VPC peering quickly becomes a management burden. In this lesson we’ll build intuition for why a hub simplifies many-to-many connectivity, and how Transit Gateway provides attachments, route tables, associations, and propagations to make routing predictable. You will see a simple numerical example that shows how peering scales poorly, then we’ll contrast that with the hub-and-spoke model that reduces connections to a single attachment per VPC. Finally, we’ll highlight a couple of common mistakes to avoid, like treating TGW route tables exactly like VPC route tables and failing to plan CIDR blocks. Introduction to AWS Transit Gateway

Understand how Transit Gateway reduces peering complexity, supports transitive routing, and centralizes inter-VPC and hybrid connectivity.

In this lesson

You will compare mesh peering and hub-and-spoke, learn TGW components, and see a shared-services example plus common pitfalls to avoid.

Why it matters

Centralized routing reduces operational overhead and enables scalable multi-account and hybrid network architectures using a single regional hub.

screens.title: Why VPC Peering Doesn't Scale
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: VPC peering creates a direct, one-to-one network connection between two VPCs. That simplicity makes peering attractive at small scale, but it leads to combinatorial growth when many VPCs must interconnect. The mathematical formula is N times N minus one, divided by two. If you have five VPCs, that becomes five times four over two, which equals ten peering connections. For ten VPCs the number grows to forty-five; for fifteen VPCs it's one hundred and five. Beyond the arithmetic, each peering link requires independent lifecycle management, distinct route table entries, and verification of non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Operational tasks multiply: creating, auditing, and updating 45 peerings is far slower and more error-prone than managing a set of attachments to a central hub. A common misconception is that peering is always cheaper because it's simple; in reality the hidden operational cost of many peering connections — change windows, access controls, and troubleshooting — often outweighs the initial simplicity. Consider a scenario where one shared service needs access from many app VPCs: with peering you add many individual connections, but with a hub you attach each VPC once and control access centrally. How would this arithmetic change your design decisions?

keyIdea.title: Peering cost
keyIdea.text: Peering grows as N*(N-1)/2 and leads to high operational overhead even if individual connections are simple.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Why VPC Peering Doesn't Scale
Comparison

Mesh peering vs operational reality

Peering gives direct connectivity but scales poorly in connection count and operations.

# Peering count formula
N = number of VPCs
peering_connections = N * (N - 1) / 2

# Examples
N = 5  -> 5*4/2 = 10
N = 10 -> 10*9/2 = 45
N = 15 -> 15*14/2 = 105
Example
A shared-services VPC needing connections from 10 app VPCs would require 10 peering links to reach each app VPC — and additional peerings between apps if they also need east-west traffic.
Common misconception
Some assume peering remains simplest as you grow. In practice, operational overhead and route management make peering unsustainable past a small number of VPCs.
Consequences
  • Many route table entries across accounts and VPCs
  • Harder auditing and change coordination
  • No native transitive routing through a peering connection
Key takeaway

Use the peering formula as a threshold: when connections and operations become the bottleneck, consider a Transit Gateway hub.

screens.title: What is AWS Transit Gateway?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub that centralizes connectivity across VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect Gateways. Define it as a managed, scalable hub that provides transitive routing between attached networks; attachments connect endpoints to the TGW and TGW route tables determine where traffic goes. This setup replaces mesh peering with a hub-and-spoke model: each spoke attaches to the TGW once, and the TGW forwards traffic based on its route tables. A concrete example: rather than creating 45 peerings for ten VPCs, you create ten attachments to a single Transit Gateway and configure route tables so traffic can flow between any two spokes when permitted. Transit Gateway is regional, highly available, and owned at the account level; it can be shared with other accounts via AWS Resource Access Manager. A common misunderstanding is to expect TGW to automatically resolve all routing conflicts — it doesn’t. You still plan unique CIDR ranges and control what routes are propagated or associated to each TGW route table. The practical benefit is dramatic reduction in connection count and improved central control over inter-VPC traffic.

keyIdea.title: TGW defined
keyIdea.text: A managed, regional transit hub providing attachments and TGW route tables for centralized, transitive routing between networks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is AWS Transit Gateway?
Definition

Transit Gateway

A managed regional hub that attaches VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect Gateways and routes traffic between them using TGW route tables.

Attachment
A logical connection from a VPC, VPN, or Direct Connect Gateway into the Transit Gateway.
TGW route table
Routes that determine how traffic moves between attachments; supports association and propagation.
Concrete example
Ten VPCs attach once to a TGW instead of creating 45 peering connections. TGW route tables control which attachments can reach each other.
Why choose TGW?
  • Simplified connection count and centralized routing
  • Built-in transitive routing between attachments
  • Supports hybrid links like Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect
Misconception check
TGW is not a magic resolver for CIDR overlap. Unique CIDR planning remains critical and propagations must be managed intentionally.

screens.title: Attachments: Types and Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Attachments are the logical connectivity points that link networks into the Transit Gateway. There are several attachment types: VPC attachments for AWS VPCs, VPN attachments for Site-to-Site VPN connections, and Direct Connect Gateway attachments for private connectivity from on-premises. Each attachment is a boundary where traffic enters or leaves the TGW and is represented as a logical entity in the TGW configuration. Ownership and account boundaries matter: attachments are created in the account that owns the resource and, if the TGW is shared, attachments can be accepted or auto-accepted depending on TGW settings. A concrete scenario: your central network account owns the TGW and you accept VPC attachments from application accounts via AWS Resource Access Manager; each application team creates their VPC attachment and the network team manages TGW route tables. A common operational pitfall is unclear attachment ownership which leads to coordination delays when establishing associations or propagations. Always document who creates attachments, who associates them to route tables, and who authorizes propagations to avoid configuration drift or unexpected traffic paths. Attachments: Types and Ownership means attachments are logical entry/exit points to the tgw; types include vpc, vpn, and direct connect gateway, and ownership influences provisioning and acceptance.. In practical terms, vpc, vpn, and direct connect gateway attachments and what they represent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Attachments are logical entry/exit points to the TGW; types include VPC, VPN, and Direct Connect Gateway, and ownership influences provisioning and acceptance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Attachments: Types and Ownership
Definition

Attachments

Logical connections from resources into the Transit Gateway. They represent where traffic enters or leaves the TGW.

VPC attachment
Connects a VPC to the TGW so that its subnets can send and receive routed traffic.
VPN attachment
Represents a Site-to-Site VPN connection from on-premises to the TGW.
Direct Connect Gateway
Used for private, high-bandwidth connections via Direct Connect.
Operational notes
  • Attachments are created by resource owners; TGW owner controls accept/auto-accept options.
  • Document attachment ownership and who configures associations/propagations.
  • Auto-accept shared attachments is a setting to streamline multi-account setups.
Scenario
Central network account owns the TGW. App teams create VPC attachments and request acceptance. Network team manages TGW route tables and associations.
Key takeaway
Clear ownership and attachment workflows prevent delays and misconfigurations when integrating many accounts and teams.

screens.title: Transit Gateway Route Tables
screens.narratorSegment: Transit Gateway route tables control how traffic flows between attachments. Think of them as routing constructs that point destinations to attachments rather than to individual network interfaces. Routes can be added statically or learned via propagation from attachments such as VPCs or VPNs. When an attachment is associated with a TGW route table, traffic coming from that attachment consults the associated table to find the appropriate next hop. Propagation, by contrast, advertises the CIDR routes from an attachment into a specific TGW route table so other attachments can reach those networks. A concrete example: VPC Attachment A propagates 10.0.0.0/16 into Route Table 1; Route Table 1 then has a route to send traffic destined for 10.0.0.0/16 to Attachment A. A common misconception is to treat TGW tables like VPC route tables that resolve to ENIs; instead, TGW routes resolve to attachments. Practically, design route tables to reflect trust and inspection boundaries — for example, associate app attachments to a route table that forwards traffic to a security VPC attachment before allowing broader access. This separation makes policy and inspection simpler at scale.

keyIdea.title: TGW routing
keyIdea.text: TGW route tables route between attachments; use associations for per-attachment table selection and propagations to advertise attachment routes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Transit Gateway Route Tables
Core Concept

TGW route tables

Routes point destinations to attachments. Associations choose which table an attachment uses; propagations add routes from attachments into tables.

# Example TGW route entries (illustrative)
Destination        Target Attachment
10.0.0.0/16       -> vpc-attach-A
10.1.0.0/16       -> vpc-attach-B
0.0.0.0/0         -> vpn-attach-1 (for on-prem connectivity)

# Propagation: vpc-attach-A advertises 10.0.0.0/16 into Route Table 1
# Association: app-attach-1 associated with Route Table 1 uses those routes
Example
Associate application attachments to a table that forwards to a security VPC attachment for inspection before allowing east-west traffic.
Misconception
TGW routes resolve to attachments, not ENIs or instances. Plan attachments and propagations accordingly.
Propagation vs Association
  • Association: ties an attachment to a specific TGW route table for inbound traffic selection
  • Propagation: advertises routes from an attachment into a TGW route table so others can reach it
Key takeaway
Design TGW route tables to match trust zones and inspection points; use propagation controls to avoid over-sharing routes.

screens.title: Associations and Propagations
screens.narratorSegment: Associations and propagations are the two configuration levers that control TGW route tables. Start with a definition: an association links an attachment to a route table so that traffic arriving from that attachment consults that table for forwarding decisions. Propagation, in turn, takes prefixes learned from an attachment — such as a VPC CIDR or routes learned from a VPN — and inserts them into a specific TGW route table. Imagine three steps in a common workflow. First, create the attachments for your VPCs and VPNs. Second, decide which attachments should be associated to which TGW route tables based on trust or inspection requirements. Third, enable propagation from attachments whose routes should be auto-learned into particular tables. A concrete example: an app VPC attachment is associated with Route Table A, while a shared-services VPC attachment propagates its CIDR into Route Table A so the app VPC can reach shared services without adding static routes. A frequent error is enabling propagation to multiple tables without restricting associations, which can unintentionally expose routes. Always design associations and propagations together to enforce principle of least privilege in routing.

keyIdea.title: Routing controls
keyIdea.text: Use associations to choose a table for inbound attachment traffic and propagations to advertise attachment routes into chosen tables; plan both together.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Associations and Propagations
Process

Associations & Propagations

Two actions define how attachments and route tables share route information and decide forwarding behavior.

Step 1
Create attachments for your VPCs, VPNs, or Direct Connect Gateways.
Step 2
Associate attachments to TGW route tables to choose the routing context for incoming traffic.
Step 3
Enable propagation so that attachment CIDRs or learned routes are advertised into chosen route tables.
Example scenario
App attachments associated with Route Table A. Shared-services attachment propagates its CIDR into Route Table A so apps reach shared services without extra static routes.
Common mistake
Enabling broad propagation without careful associations can expose internal networks across attachments unintentionally.
Pro tip
Group attachments by trust level and create separate TGW route tables for inspection vs. production traffic to minimize blast radius.

screens.title: Shared Services VPC Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: A shared services VPC hosts centralized functions like Active Directory, DNS resolvers, or logging. Historically, each application VPC would peer to the shared-services VPC directly, producing many peering connections. With Transit Gateway, the shared-services VPC simply attaches to the TGW and its routes are propagated into the appropriate TGW route tables. Application VPCs attach to the TGW and are associated with the route tables that include the shared-services routes. In practice this means fewer connections to create and maintain, consolidated routing decisions, and easier centralized security controls. A concrete example: ten application VPCs need DNS and AD. Instead of creating 10 peerings to the shared-services VPC, each app VPC creates one attachment and the TGW route table propagates the shared-services CIDR to those tables. A typical operational consideration is to restrict which TGW route tables receive the shared-services propagation so you don't inadvertently expose internal services to environments that shouldn't access them. This pattern reduces configuration churn while enabling centralized monitoring and enforcement. Shared Services VPC Pattern means attach both application vpcs and a shared-services vpc to the tgw and use route tables to control access without many peerings.. In practical terms, centralizing common services using tgw attachments and routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Shared Services VPC Pattern
Use Case

Shared services via TGW

Centralize common services and control which applications can reach them using TGW route tables and propagations.

Before (peering)
Each app VPC peers directly with shared-services VPC — many connections and route entries to manage.
After (TGW)
All VPCs attach once to the TGW; shared-services attachment propagates routes to selected TGW route tables.
Concrete scenario
Ten application VPCs and one shared-services VPC: ten attachments instead of ten peerings for each app; route tables manage access.
Operational tip
Limit propagation of shared-services CIDRs to only the TGW route tables used by approved app environments to reduce exposure.
Key takeaway
TGW reduces connection count and centralizes security controls for shared services while preserving control over who can reach those services.

screens.title: Inter-Account Connectivity and Resource Sharing
screens.narratorSegment: Large organizations often centralize network ownership in a dedicated account and share the Transit Gateway with other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager. This ownership model simplifies governance because a single team manages TGW route tables, associations, and propagations while application teams create and attach their VPCs. Resource Access Manager enables the TGW owner to share the TGW resource without transferring ownership of the underlying Transit Gateway. A concrete example: a central networking account owns the TGW and configures route tables for security and production zones; multiple application accounts attach their VPCs to the shared TGW and follow the association rules the network team sets. Practical considerations include configuring auto-accept shared attachments if you want attachments to be accepted automatically, or requiring manual acceptance for stricter control. Also, ensure clear IAM and governance procedures so attachments and route changes are auditable. Misunderstandings often arise from thinking sharing removes the need for coordination — in reality it centralizes control but still requires defined operational processes between teams. Inter-Account Connectivity and Resource Sharing means host the tgw in a central account and use aws ram to share it, enabling centralized route management while application accounts attach their vpcs.. In practical terms, owning the tgw in a central account and sharing it with application accounts. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Operational Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting Transit Gateway, teams frequently make a few predictable mistakes. First, treating TGW route tables the same way as VPC route tables causes confusion; TGW routes point to attachments, not individual network interfaces inside a VPC, so route planning and next hops are at the attachment level. Second, inadequate CIDR planning leads to overlapping networks across attachments, which TGW cannot resolve automatically and which will cause routing conflicts. Third, enabling broad propagation without matching association discipline can open unwanted access paths. Best practices follow directly from these mistakes: plan unique CIDRs for all connected networks, design TGW route tables around trust boundaries and inspection points, and control propagation so only intended routes are advertised. Operationally, document attachment ownership and association responsibilities and consider using separate TGW route tables for production, staging, and security inspection to limit blast radius. A final tip: apply principle of least privilege to route exposure — only propagate and associate what is necessary. These practices reduce surprises and make TGW a reliable backbone for multi-VPC and hybrid networks. fullNarratorScript:
As your AWS footprint grows, individual VPC peering quickly becomes a management burden. In this lesson we’ll build intuition for why a hub simplifies many-to-many connectivity, and how Transit Gateway provides attachments, route tables, associations, and propagations to make routing predictable. You will see a simple numerical example that shows how peering scales poorly, then we’ll contrast that with the hub-and-spoke model that reduces connections to a single attachment per VPC. We’ll also describe the core TGW components and a practical shared-services scenario where centralized routing and policy enforcement reduce complexity. Finally, we’ll highlight a couple of common mistakes to avoid, like treating TGW route tables exactly like VPC route tables and failing to plan CIDR blocks. By the end of this chapter you will understand when Transit Gateway is appropriate and what operational changes it introduces, so you can decide whether a hub-and-spoke design will simplify networking in your environment.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why VPC peering does not scale and how Transit Gateway changes the operational model. You will identify Transit Gateway’s core components — attachments, route tables, associations, and propagations — and understand how these pieces work together to provide transitive routing between attached networks. You will recognize common enterprise use cases such as shared-services VPCs and inter-account connectivity via resource sharing, and you will know the practical design considerations like CIDR planning and least-privilege route exposure. Each objective links a specific skill with a real-world reason: fewer connections to manage, clearer routing policies, and centralized inspection or security VPCs. You will leave able to describe both the mechanical pieces and the operational benefits, so you can judge when to adopt a TGW-based hub-and-spoke design.

These objectives are practical. First, when you explain peering limits, you’ll use the N times N minus one over two formula to reason about connection count and management overhead. That gives you a clear trigger for considering Transit Gateway. Second, by describing TGW components you learn to map architecture elements — attachments for connectivity endpoints and TGW route tables for traffic flow — to operational actions like association and propagation choices. Third, identifying use cases means you can choose a central network account and share the TGW where appropriate, enabling inter-account traffic without peer proliferation. Fourth, applying hub-and-spoke helps you plan CIDR assignments and route exposure so you avoid overlap and unintended reachability. Each skill matters because it reduces change windows, makes auditing simpler, and supports centralized security controls. Practice the console walkthrough in the activity to reinforce these skills and verify that you can find attachments, route tables, associations, and propagations in the AWS VPC console.

Start with a clear definition: VPC peering creates a direct, one-to-one network connection between two VPCs. That simplicity makes peering attractive at small scale, but it leads to combinatorial growth when many VPCs must interconnect. The mathematical formula is N times N minus one, divided by two. If you have five VPCs, that becomes five times four over two, which equals ten peering connections. For ten VPCs the number grows to forty-five; for fifteen VPCs it's one hundred and five. Beyond the arithmetic, each peering link requires independent lifecycle management, distinct route table entries, and verification of non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Operational tasks multiply: creating, auditing, and updating 45 peerings is far slower and more error-prone than managing a set of attachments to a central hub. A common misconception is that peering is always cheaper because it's simple; in reality the hidden operational cost of many peering connections — change windows, access controls, and troubleshooting — often outweighs the initial simplicity. Consider a scenario where one shared service needs access from many app VPCs: with peering you add many individual connections, but with a hub you attach each VPC once and control access centrally. How would this arithmetic change your design decisions?

AWS Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub that centralizes connectivity across VPCs, VPNs, and Direct Connect Gateways. Define it as a managed, scalable hub that provides transitive routing between attached networks; attachments connect endpoints to the TGW and TGW route tables determine where traffic goes. This setup replaces mesh peering with a hub-and-spoke model: each spoke attaches to the TGW once, and the TGW forwards traffic based on its route tables. A concrete example: rather than creating 45 peerings for ten VPCs, you create ten attachments to a single Transit Gateway and configure route tables so traffic can flow between any two spokes when permitted. Transit Gateway is regional, highly available, and owned at the account level; it can be shared with other accounts via AWS Resource Access Manager. A common misunderstanding is to expect TGW to automatically resolve all routing conflicts — it doesn’t. You still plan unique CIDR ranges and control what routes are propagated or associated to each TGW route table. The practical benefit is dramatic reduction in connection count and improved central control over inter-VPC traffic.

Attachments are the logical connectivity points that link networks into the Transit Gateway. There are several attachment types: VPC attachments for AWS VPCs, VPN attachments for Site-to-Site VPN connections, and Direct Connect Gateway attachments for private connectivity from on-premises. Each attachment is a boundary where traffic enters or leaves the TGW and is represented as a logical entity in the TGW configuration. Ownership and account boundaries matter: attachments are created in the account that owns the resource and, if the TGW is shared, attachments can be accepted or auto-accepted depending on TGW settings. A concrete scenario: your central network account owns the TGW and you accept VPC attachments from application accounts via AWS Resource Access Manager; each application team creates their VPC attachment and the network team manages TGW route tables. A common operational pitfall is unclear attachment ownership which leads to coordination delays when establishing associations or propagations. Always document who creates attachments, who associates them to route tables, and who authorizes propagations to avoid configuration drift or unexpected traffic paths. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Transit Gateway route tables control how traffic flows between attachments. Think of them as routing constructs that point destinations to attachments rather than to individual network interfaces. Routes can be added statically or learned via propagation from attachments such as VPCs or VPNs. When an attachment is associated with a TGW route table, traffic coming from that attachment consults the associated table to find the appropriate next hop. Propagation, by contrast, advertises the CIDR routes from an attachment into a specific TGW route table so other attachments can reach those networks. A concrete example: VPC Attachment A propagates 10.0.0.0/16 into Route Table 1; Route Table 1 then has a route to send traffic destined for 10.0.0.0/16 to Attachment A. A common misconception is to treat TGW tables like VPC route tables that resolve to ENIs; instead, TGW routes resolve to attachments. Practically, design route tables to reflect trust and inspection boundaries — for example, associate app attachments to a route table that forwards traffic to a security VPC attachment before allowing broader access. This separation makes policy and inspection simpler at scale.

Associations and propagations are the two configuration levers that control TGW route tables. Start with a definition: an association links an attachment to a route table so that traffic arriving from that attachment consults that table for forwarding decisions. Propagation, in turn, takes prefixes learned from an attachment — such as a VPC CIDR or routes learned from a VPN — and inserts them into a specific TGW route table. Imagine three steps in a common workflow. First, create the attachments for your VPCs and VPNs. Second, decide which attachments should be associated to which TGW route tables based on trust or inspection requirements. Third, enable propagation from attachments whose routes should be auto-learned into particular tables. A concrete example: an app VPC attachment is associated with Route Table A, while a shared-services VPC attachment propagates its CIDR into Route Table A so the app VPC can reach shared services without adding static routes. A frequent error is enabling propagation to multiple tables without restricting associations, which can unintentionally expose routes. Always design associations and propagations together to enforce principle of least privilege in routing.

A shared services VPC hosts centralized functions like Active Directory, DNS resolvers, or logging. Historically, each application VPC would peer to the shared-services VPC directly, producing many peering connections. With Transit Gateway, the shared-services VPC simply attaches to the TGW and its routes are propagated into the appropriate TGW route tables. Application VPCs attach to the TGW and are associated with the route tables that include the shared-services routes. In practice this means fewer connections to create and maintain, consolidated routing decisions, and easier centralized security controls. A concrete example: ten application VPCs need DNS and AD. Instead of creating 10 peerings to the shared-services VPC, each app VPC creates one attachment and the TGW route table propagates the shared-services CIDR to those tables. A typical operational consideration is to restrict which TGW route tables receive the shared-services propagation so you don't inadvertently expose internal services to environments that shouldn't access them. This pattern reduces configuration churn while enabling centralized monitoring and enforcement.
